title: NICB Warns Illinois Residents of Storm-Chasing Contractor Fraud After 140 Tornadoes, a Derecho and Flooding
summary: On June 18, 2026 the National Insurance Crime Bureau warned Illinois homeowners and businesses about fraudulent contractors after a derecho, a tornado outbreak and flooding; the state had recorded 140 tornadoes against an annual average of 54.
description:
A run of severe weather in Illinois has prompted a fraud warning from the insurance industry's crime-fighting body. On June 18, 2026, the National Insurance Crime Bureau (NICB) urged Illinois residents and business owners to watch for fraudulent contractors in communities hit by storms. The bureau said the state had seen, over about two weeks, a derecho that caused widespread wind damage across northern Illinois, a tornado outbreak that damaged homes and businesses, and heavy rain that raised flooding concerns in parts of the Chicago metropolitan area. This article is based on the NICB's alert. An earlier version of this article included a figure for annual US severe convective storm losses that we could not verify against the alert, and it has been removed. This is general information, not legal or insurance advice.

How unusual is the weather? The NICB reported that Illinois had recorded 140 tornadoes so far in 2026, compared with an average of 54 in a year, and said this made it the state with the most tornadoes in the country. That is more than two and a half times the annual average, reached before midsummer. Later reporting by Live Insurance News, published in October 2026, cited a preliminary count of about 192 tornadoes for the year, a record for the state, and said State Farm claims data showed Illinois homeowner claims running well above the ten-year average. We have not independently confirmed those later figures, which may change as the National Weather Service completes its surveys, so treat them as preliminary.

Why does fraud follow storms? NICB President and CEO David J. Glawe said that this is when home and business owners must be most vigilant, noting that fraudsters exploit people who are eager to start recovering. After a storm, demand for roofers, tree services and repairers outstrips supply. People want a tarp on the roof, a window boarded up or a tree removed immediately. That urgency, combined with confusion about insurance claims, gives dishonest operators room to work. They may take a deposit and never return, do poor work that fails later, or inflate a claim by adding damage that did not occur.

What are the warning signs? The NICB lists several red flags. Be wary of solicitors who appear immediately after a storm, particularly those who knock on doors, call or approach online. Be cautious of anyone who claims to be affiliated with your insurer without proof, who offers a free inspection as a hook, who demands cash payment, or who pressures you to sign at once to get a special deal. Do not sign a contract with blank spaces. Do not pay the full price before work begins. Be suspicious of any offer to waive your deductible, because an insurer will not expect you to pay your deductible up front or over the phone, and a contractor who promises to absorb it may be inflating the claim to cover the cost, which can amount to insurance fraud. Finally, be careful with an Assignment of Benefits, a document that transfers your rights under your insurance policy to the contractor. Read it carefully, because it can affect your control of the claim.

What should homeowners do first? The NICB advises contacting your insurer first if you suspect storm damage. Read all documents before sending them to your insurer. Do not let a contractor interpret your policy or discourage you from calling your insurer. Do not give personal information to callers until they confirm a claim number. Where emergency repairs are needed to prevent further damage, such as covering a hole in the roof, check your policy and keep receipts and photographs, because most policies require reasonable steps to protect the property and may reimburse them.

How should you choose a contractor? Get multiple estimates and avoid rushing. Ask for references and research the company. The NICB suggests recording the salesperson's driver's licence and vehicle plate numbers, and being wary of out-of-state contractor licences or vehicle registrations. Reject unsolicited offers. Get everything in writing, including the cost, scope of work, timelines, guarantees and payment schedule. Never sign a completion certificate until the work is actually finished and you are satisfied with it, because insurers and lenders may treat that certificate as proof that the job is done. A free downloadable checklist is available on the NICB website.

What does the Illinois state guidance add? The Live Insurance News report notes that the Illinois Department of Insurance, like most state regulators, advises homeowners to verify a contractor's licence independently, to contact the insurer first so an adjuster can document damage, and then to get two to three estimates from licensed contractors. It also refers to the Illinois Home Repair and Remodeling Act, which it says requires written contracts for repair work over $1,000. Readers should confirm these requirements with the department and the statute, as we have relied on a secondary report for them.

How can fraud be reported? Suspected insurance fraud can be reported to the NICB by calling 800-835-6422 or by submitting a form on the bureau's website. The NICB says it works with more than 1,200 property-casualty insurers and other member organisations.

What are the wider implications? Repeated severe convective storms put pressure on household budgets, insurers and local building trades. Fraud adds to the cost, because dishonest claims and shoddy repairs raise losses that are ultimately reflected in premiums across a market. For consumers, the most protective habits are simple: call your insurer before you sign anything, document the damage, get several quotes, and take your time. For communities, local officials and consumer groups often reinforce these messages after a disaster.

This article summarises an industry alert and secondary reports and is not legal or insurance advice. Contact your insurer and the Illinois Department of Insurance for advice on your own claim.
image_alt: Storm damage to a residential property requiring insurance claim (illustrative)
key_points: The NICB issued its alert on June 18, 2026 from Oak Brook, Illinois, after two weeks of storms that included a derecho in northern Illinois, a tornado outbreak and flooding concerns in the Chicago area.
Illinois had recorded 140 tornadoes so far in 2026, against a state average of 54 a year, the most of any state according to the NICB; later reports cited a higher preliminary count.

Red flags include post-storm solicitors, unverifiable claims of insurer affiliation, 'free' inspections, cash demands, pressure to sign, blank contract spaces, offers to waive deductibles and requests for an Assignment of Benefits.
The NICB advises contacting your insurer first, getting multiple estimates, checking references and licences, and never paying in full or signing a completion certificate before work is finished.
Suspected fraud can be reported to the NICB on 800-835-6422 or through nicb.org; the bureau works with more than 1,200 property-casualty insurers and other member organisations.
why_it_matters: After a disaster, homeowners are under pressure to act fast and are easy targets. Knowing the common tactics, and sequencing a claim correctly, can prevent a second loss on top of the storm damage.

title: India Opens Insurance to 100% Foreign Ownership Under the Automatic Route, With a Resident Leadership Condition and a 20% Cap for LIC
summary: Reported on May 2, 2026, the government allowed up to 100% foreign investment in insurance companies through the automatic route, requiring at least one resident Indian citizen as chair, managing director or CEO, while foreign investment in LIC stays at 20%.
description:
India has removed the foreign ownership ceiling on insurance companies. Business Today reported on May 2, 2026 that the Centre allowed 100% foreign direct investment (FDI) in insurance companies through the automatic route, citing the Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade's Press Note 1 (2026 Series). Under the press note, foreign investment, including portfolio investment, is permitted automatically, subject to regulatory clearance from the Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India (IRDAI). This article summarises that report and related coverage. An earlier version of this article cited a statutory order number and a market-penetration figure that we could not verify against the source, so they have been removed. The article is general information and not legal or investment advice.

What changed? Foreign ownership in Indian insurers was previously limited. The cap was 26% until 2015, 49% until 2021 and 74% after that, a progression that readers will find in earlier reporting on the sector. The new rule lifts it to 100% for insurance companies, and does so under the automatic route, meaning that investors do not need prior government approval, though IRDAI's own approvals still apply. The report notes the change aligns with the Insurance Laws (Amendment) Act, 2025, most provisions of which took effect on February 5, 2026.

What conditions apply? The report lists three conditions that matter. First, insurers with foreign investment must appoint at least one resident Indian citizen as chairperson, managing director or chief executive officer. Second, any increase in foreign shareholding must follow Reserve Bank of India pricing guidelines under the Foreign Exchange Management Act. Third, the investment remains subject to IRDAI's regulatory clearance. The report does not describe other safeguards, such as requirements for local directors, and we do not infer any.

What about LIC? The Life Insurance Corporation of India, the state-owned insurer, is treated separately. Foreign investment in LIC remains at 20% under the automatic route, under its own framework. That means the reform does not open the largest life insurer to majority foreign ownership.

What about intermediaries? The report says the 100% limit also covers insurance intermediaries: brokers, reinsurance brokers, corporate agents, third-party administrators, surveyors, loss assessors, managing general agents and insurance repositories, all subject to IRDAI norms. Business Today notes that full foreign ownership of intermediaries was already permitted in 2020. Banks acting as intermediaries keep the sector caps for their primary business where more than 50% of their revenue comes from non-insurance activities, and majority foreign-owned intermediaries must be incorporated as limited companies under the Companies Act, 2013.

Why is the government doing this? The report says the move should attract global insurers, improve competition and raise insurance penetration, especially in underserved segments. Insurance penetration, the ratio of premiums to the size of the economy, is lower in India than in many comparable markets, and the government has spoken about extending cover widely over the coming decades. We have not verified the exact current penetration figure, so we do not state it. More capital allows insurers to underwrite more business, because regulatory solvency rules tie the amount of risk an insurer can take to its capital.

What approvals followed? At its 134th meeting on March 9, 2026, IRDAI registered Allianz Jio Reinsurance Limited as a reinsurer and Kiwi General Insurance Limited as a general insurer, according to the report. These approvals came before the FDI press note and show the regulator licensing new entrants as the Act took effect.

Who might benefit and who might lose? Foreign insurers with joint ventures in India could, subject to approvals, raise their stakes, and new entrants could set up wholly owned subsidiaries. Domestic partners might sell down. Competition could lead to lower prices and new products for customers, but it could also challenge smaller insurers. The report does not predict which firms will act, and any claims about specific deals should wait for filings or announcements.

What are the risks? Full foreign ownership raises policy questions about governance, data, policyholder protection and the interests of Indian shareholders in joint ventures. The resident leadership rule and IRDAI's oversight are the main safeguards named in the report. Regulators can also use solvency, fit-and-proper tests and disclosure rules. For policyholders, the practical question is whether services improve and claims are paid fairly, and that depends on supervision as much as on ownership.

What should readers watch? Whether foreign groups announce stake increases or new subsidiaries; how IRDAI handles clearances and what conditions it attaches; and the effect on competition and prices. The regulator's draft framework for making regulations, covered in a related article on this site, will also shape how the new rules are consulted on.

This article summarises a press report and is not legal or investment advice. Investors should consult the official Press Note, the Foreign Exchange Management Rules and IRDAI's regulations.
image_alt: India financial sector insurance market liberalization (illustrative)
key_points: Business Today reported on May 2, 2026 that the Centre allowed 100% foreign direct investment in insurance companies through the automatic route, citing DPIIT Press Note 1 (2026 Series), subject to IRDAI regulatory clearance.
Foreign investment in the Life Insurance Corporation of India stays at 20% under the automatic route, under a separate framework.

Insurers with foreign investment must appoint at least one resident Indian citizen as chairperson, managing director or chief executive officer, and increases in foreign shareholding must follow RBI pricing guidelines under FEMA.

The 100% limit also covers brokers, reinsurance brokers, corporate agents, third-party administrators, surveyors, loss assessors, managing general agents and insurance repositories; full foreign ownership of intermediaries was already allowed in 2020.
The change aligns with the Insurance Laws (Amendment) Act, 2025, most of which took effect on February 5, 2026; on March 9, 2026 IRDAI registered Allianz Jio Reinsurance and Kiwi General Insurance.
why_it_matters: Global insurers can now take full control of Indian businesses without prior government approval, which could bring capital and competition to a market with low insurance coverage. IRDAI clearance and the resident-leadership rule remain the checkpoints.

title: MetLife Adds a Three-Year Cancellation Option to Its Guaranteed Income Annuity for Retirement Plan Participants
summary: MetLife announced on May 28, 2026 an Annuity Cancellation Option for its Guaranteed Income Program, letting plan participants cancel within the first three years of income payments and receive premiums paid minus benefits received, with no cancellation or surrender fees.
description:
MetLife has added a cancellation feature to the immediate income annuity it offers to workplace retirement plans. On May 28, 2026, the company announced an Annuity Cancellation Option for the MetLife Guaranteed Income Program, known as MGIP. According to MetLife's press release, participants in defined contribution plans who convert savings into MGIP income can cancel within the first three years of receiving payments. On cancellation they receive a refund of the premiums paid minus the benefits already received, and MetLife says there are no cancellation or surrender fees. This article summarises the company's announcement and the research it cites. An earlier version of this article described the product's reception in broader terms than the announcement supports, so those statements have been removed. Readers considering any annuity should read the contract and speak to a qualified adviser.

What is an immediate income annuity? An immediate income annuity is a contract in which a person hands an insurer a lump sum, called the premium, and in return receives a stream of regular payments that begins straight away. The payments can last for life or for a set period. Because the insurer pools the longevity risk of many customers, the income can be higher than a person could safely draw from their own savings if they wanted to be sure the money would never run out. The trade-off is that the decision has traditionally been irreversible: once the premium is paid, the money is no longer the customer's to withdraw. That loss of access is the objection MetLife is trying to address.

How does the cancellation option work? Under the design announced by MetLife, a participant who has begun receiving MGIP payments can change their mind during the first three years of income. The refund equals the premiums paid less the benefits already received. In plain terms, if someone paid a premium of a given size and has received some payments, they would get back the difference. MetLife says there are no cancellation or surrender fees. After the three-year window the annuity reverts to a standard income annuity, which means the cancellation right is a feature of the early years only. The announcement does not say how "benefits already received" are calculated in detail, whether the refund is adjusted for investment returns or interest, or how a participant would start a cancellation. Those points would be in the contract and plan documents, and we have not seen them.

Who is it for? The release describes MGIP as designed for defined contribution plan participants, such as members of employer 401(k) style plans. These are the people who must turn a pot of savings into an income, often without a pension. MetLife's head of institutional income annuities, Roberta Rafaloff, said participants want dependable income they can count on, along with the flexibility to adapt as their needs evolve. She also said the option gives participants added options and control early in retirement.

What research does MetLife cite? The company points to two studies. The first is the Employee Benefit Research Institute's 2026 Retirement Confidence Survey, which MetLife says found that more than four in five workers expressed interest in guaranteed income. The second is a 2026 paper from Goldman Sachs Asset Management, titled Decoding Retirement Income: The Retirement Saver Preference Gap, which MetLife says shows that consumers increasingly value solutions that combine reliable income with flexibility. These are cited by the insurer to support its product design, and readers should treat them as the company's framing of the research, not as independent endorsement of this product.

What else does MGIP include? According to the announcement, payment options include lifetime income or income for a specified period. Optional features include a beneficiary protection feature, under which remaining value passes to a beneficiary, and options to help income keep pace with rising costs. Each optional feature normally reduces the starting income compared with a basic contract, though the release does not give figures.

What are the open questions? The first is price. A right to get premiums back is valuable, and insurers normally build the cost of such guarantees into the payout rate. The announcement does not say whether participants who choose MGIP with the cancellation option receive a lower income than they would without it, or whether the option is included for everyone. The second is how the refund would be funded and whether the insurer's investment assumptions change when many participants might cancel. A cancellation right can create selection effects, because people are more likely to cancel if their health improves, their finances change or interest rates move in a way that makes other options look better. Insurers price for that behaviour, and the effect on income is a fair question for any adviser to ask. The third is the inflation question. A refund of premiums minus payments received is fixed in dollars. If prices rise over three years, the real value of the refund falls.

How should retirees compare it with alternatives? Someone choosing between an annuity and drawing savings from an investment portfolio is weighing certainty against flexibility. A cancellation window narrows that gap for the first three years but does not remove it. After that period, the contract is a standard annuity. A prudent comparison would look at the guaranteed income per dollar of premium with and without the option, the financial strength of the insurer, the treatment of any inflation adjustment, and the tax treatment inside the plan. Plan sponsors, which are the employers that offer the product to workers, also have fiduciary duties when choosing an annuity provider, so the option will be one of several features they weigh.

Why does it matter for the wider market? Annuities have struggled to win a large share of workplace plans despite surveys that show interest in guaranteed income. Product features aimed at flexibility, such as cancellation windows, withdrawal rights and liquidity, are one way insurers are trying to close that gap. Whether the feature changes behaviour will depend on uptake by plan sponsors, which MetLife has not reported.

This article summarises a company announcement and is not financial, legal or investment advice. Terms, availability and pricing are set by the contract and by each plan.
image_alt: Retirement income planning and annuity products (illustrative)
key_points: MetLife announced the Annuity Cancellation Option on May 28, 2026 as a feature of the MetLife Guaranteed Income Program (MGIP), an immediate income annuity designed for defined contribution plan participants.

Participants can cancel within the first three years of receiving payments and get a refund of premiums paid minus benefits already received, with no cancellation or surrender fees, according to MetLife.

MetLife cites the EBRI 2026 Retirement Confidence Survey (more than four in five workers interested in guaranteed income) and a 2026 Goldman Sachs Asset Management paper on the retirement saver preference gap.
The release does not disclose the cost of the option, how benefits received are calculated, or whether it applies to every payment option, so terms are set by the contract.
MGIP also offers lifetime or period-certain income, an optional beneficiary protection feature and options intended to help income keep pace with rising costs.
why_it_matters: Fear of an irreversible decision is one of the most common reasons retirees avoid annuities. A cancellation window tests whether a liquidity feature can bring guaranteed income into workplace plans, but the price of that flexibility is not yet public.
